I have worked these fields in Quzhou for forty years, and at sixty I know every corner of my twenty mu. With six people in my household, I must grow enough grain to eat, but I also need cash for school fees, medicine, and daily costs. That is why I keep ten mu in the wheat-maize rotation on my best flat land, five mu in cotton on the sandier patch, and five mu in chili close to the house where my family can tend and pick it.

The wheat went into the ground last October, so now that spring is starting my job is to nurse it through to harvest. I will top-dress urea at green-up and irrigate three times from my well—at regreening, at jointing, and at grain filling—because those are the stages that fix the yield. I do not till the wheat once it is growing; I just walk the rows and watch for aphids and powdery mildew, which means two pesticide sprays should be enough. After we harvest the wheat in early June, the straw comes off and I immediately rotary-till to plant hybrid maize seed. Maize in summer is thirsty at the big trumpet stage and during grain filling, so I will irrigate twice then, and spray twice for worms and leaf spot. The cotton goes in during April on that lighter soil; it needs four pesticide applications for bollworm and aphids, plus two irrigations at flowering and boll stage. The chili is transplanted in May and needs plenty of potash to set fruit well, so I give it more potassium than the other crops, along with three irrigations and three sprays for thrips and anthracnose. I use well water carefully because pumping costs diesel money, but I have learned never to let these crops go dry at the critical moments. I stick to improved varieties for wheat, cotton, and chili—seeds I know from experience—and hybrid maize, because that is what works on this plain. I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat, 550 kg per mu of maize, 250 kg per mu of seed cotton, and around 2,000 kg per mu of fresh chili. That feeds my family and leaves produce to sell.
